steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Igneous rocks form from the cooling and crystallisation of magma (intrusive) or lava (extrusive)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Intrusive igneous rocks cool slowly underground, producing large visible crystals (coarse-grained): granite, gabbro, diorite

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Extrusive igneous rocks cool rapidly at the surface, producing fine-grained or glassy textures: basalt, rhyolite, andesite, obsidian

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Granite (felsic, intrusive) = quartz + feldspar + mica; Basalt (mafic, extrusive) = pyroxene + plagioclase + olivine

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: How does cooling rate affect the texture of igneous rocks? | Q: What is the mineral composition of granite? | Q: Describe Bowen's reaction series.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Slow cooling (underground) allows time for large crystals to grow, producing coarse-grained texture (e.g. granite). Rapid cooling (at the surface) produces small crystals, giving fine-grained texture  | Quartz, orthoclase feldspar, plagioclase feldspar, and mica (biotite and/or muscovite). It is a felsic, intrusive rock. | As magma cools, minerals crystallise in a predictable order. The discontinuous branch: olivine, then pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite. The continuous branch: calcium-rich plagioclase becoming so

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Cooling rate = texture: slow = coarse, fast = fine, instant = glassy Granite (intrusive) and Rhyolite (extrusive): same composition, different texture Basalt (extrusive) and Gabbro (intrusive): same composition, different texture Bowen's series: discontinuous branch + continuous branch, know the mineral order
